abstract: Cells contain radial arrays or polar bundles of microtubules that support their main functions. Active matter made of microtubules and molecular motors can transiently assemble radial asters or form nematic structures that continuously extend and fold. Whether such networks can reach dynamic steady states, as seen in cells, is not known. Here we asked whether confining two oppositely directed motors could generate dynamic, stable and regular organizations. Microtubules alignment and polarity sorting formed linear stacks that partitioned the available space into domains enriched in one motor or the other. Motor ratio, microtubule number and length, and the size and shape of the confinement determined whether the resulting domain organizations were radial, polar, bipolar or multipolar. Similar patterns formed in living cells upon microtubule stabilization. These findings reveal regular, dynamic steady-states in confined active matter and open new ways to understand the diversity of microtubule network architectures in cells.
